extracted.intended_audience: employers, workers, independent businesses, labor and employment attorneys, HR and compliance officers, and other regulated stakeholders seeking DOL guidance on FLSA worker classification
extracted.subtask_description: Determining whether a worker is an employee or an independent contractor under the FLSA using the Department's multifactor economic reality test and related regulatory guidance. Emphasizes a totality-of-the-circumstances analysis and explains how individual factors should be applied and interpreted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Totality-of-the-circumstances economic reality test
rubrics_metrics.description: The ultimate inquiry is whether, as a matter of economic reality, the worker is economically dependent on the employer for work (and is thus an employee) or is in business for themself (and is thus an independent contractor). The Department returns to a multifactor totality-of-the-circumstances analysis in which the factors do not have a predetermined weight and no factor or factors are dispositive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use 'core factors' or give predetermined weighting to any single factor; consider all factors in view of the economic reality of the whole activity. The examples in the preamble are aids for applying the discussion of each proposed factor and are not intended to illustrate application of the full totality-of-the-circumstances test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investment factor
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare the worker's investments and the employer's investments to determine whether the worker is making similar types of investments as the employer that suggest the worker is operating independently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on comparing the nature (not just size) of investments. Minor, job-specific purchases (e.g., occasional small drafting tools used only to complete specific jobs for an employer) that do not further the worker's independent business weigh against independent-contractor status. Examples should be aligned (e.g., both using 'commercial design firm' as employer) to avoid confusion; size alone is not dispositive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integral (centrality) factor
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the tasks performed by the worker are core to the functioning of the employer's business — i.e., activities the employer 'could not function without the service performed by the workers.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a common-sense approach courts have used to identify tasks that are central or important. Example: a farm selling tomatoes could not function without tomato pickers (integral), whereas non-payroll accounting support is more peripheral. The integral factor is about being integral to the potential employer's business rather than being part of an integrated unit of production.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opportunity for profit or loss factor
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the worker has a real opportunity for profit or risk of loss from the work, including through business decisions such as marketing, price-setting, and other business-like choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affirmative marketing or other business-like actions may be probative of being in business for oneself, but traditional marketing is not required to be classified as an independent contractor. The inclusion or absence of marketing or other facts in an example does not imply those facts are always more or less probative. Consider the worker's actual ability to affect profit/loss (pricing, business decisions), not just superficial indicators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skill and initiative factor
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate the worker's specialized skills and the use of those skills to exercise business-like initiative consistent with being in business for themself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specialized skills can point toward independent-contractor status, but specialized skills alone are not sufficient. The critical issue is whether the worker uses those skills to contribute to business-like initiative (e.g., marketing those skills). Workers who lack specialized skills may nonetheless be independent contractors, but this factor is less likely to point that way in such circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control factor (including scheduling, supervision, price-setting, ability to work for others)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine the degree of control the employer exercises over the worker, including scheduling, remote supervision, price setting, and constraints on the worker's ability to work for others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The final rule provides broader discussion of scheduling, remote supervision, price-setting, and the ability to work for others under the control factor. Consider reserved rights to control (the employer's retained or contractual rights) as relevant evidence of control rather than minimizing their relevance. Control manifested through algorithmic supervision or the employer's collection and use of data about worker performance can also be probative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reserved rights to control (consideration of retained or contractual control)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department allows consideration of an employer's reserved rights to control work (including contractual or regulatory controls) when assessing the control factor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rejects prior minimization of retained rights (as in the 2021 IC Rule); reserved rights, even if not exercised, may be probative of control. The Department declined requests to add extensive context about reserved control to examples but acknowledges it is relevant and may be rare in practice; examples were drafted to address common themes, not exhaustively catalog reserved-control scenarios.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permanency / exclusivity factor
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider permanency of the relationship and any exclusivity that constrains the worker's ability to work for others (e.g., the number of hours or days the worker needs to work for one employer), which bears on economic dependence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclusivity and constraints on the ability to work for others are considered in the context of the permanency factor; such constraints may indicate economic dependence and employee status, depending on the totality of circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of investment and opportunity-for-profit factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Investment and opportunity for profit or loss are separate factors to be evaluated independently rather than being combined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The final rule returns investment to its longstanding framing as its own separate factor; this differs from the 2021 IC Rule which had treated investment as a component of opportunity for profit or loss.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and limits of illustrative examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples in the preamble are aids to apply the discussion of each factor and are not designed to illustrate application of the full economic reality test or to present multifactor outcomes for specific industries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples are intended to provide general guidance and to illustrate the basic analysis under a single factor; they are not definitive statements about ultimate classification. The Department declines to add industry-specific or multifactor examples in the rule because such examples could be misread as prejudging outcomes, reduce general applicability, or require excessive factual detail. Examples reside in the preamble (not regulatory text) to capstone each factor discussion; industry-specific or results-oriented examples are better addressed in subregulatory guidance if needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of algorithmic supervision and data-collection as facets of control
rubrics_metrics.description: Where relevant, employer collection of data about worker performance and algorithmic supervision can be part of the economic reality analysis under the control factor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department agrees these topics are highly relevant for some workers. While examples were not expanded to include algorithmic control or data-collection scenarios in the final rule, such facets are explicitly recognized as potentially impacting the economic reality test and should be considered where present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guidance against treating particular facts as always dispositive
rubrics_metrics.description: No single fact or small subset of facts should be treated as always determinative of worker classification; the analysis must consider all relevant facts within the multifactor framework.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department intentionally drafted examples to avoid giving the impression that certain facts are always less or always more probative. The final rule cautions against providing results-oriented, industry-specific examples that might imply a single factor determines the ultimate classification.
